data.title: Zakon sudnyj ljudem – the law code of Great Moravia
data.excerpt: No detailed body of law has survived from the times before Great Moravia, yet Frankish annals themselves record that the Slavs had laws and customs of their own. The Zakon sudnyj ljudem, the oldest known Slavic legal monument, was drawn up for Great Moravia by Constantine and Methodius at the request of Prince Rastislav – 33 articles modelled on the Byzantine Ecloga, which served only as a supplement to the existing customary law. The text of the code follows.

children.text: No detailed body of law has survived from the times before the Great Moravian state came into being, of the kind we know, for example, from East Francia, Byzantium and so on. It may nevertheless be assumed that a certain body of law of their own, probably largely customary, took shape in Nitra and in Moravia also in the times preceding the rise of Great Moravia. Indirect evidence for this is the entry in the Annals of Fulda for the year 849 about the negotiations of the Franks with the Slavs of Bohemia, for which men versed in Slavic laws and customs were appointed. It is important that the chronicler distinguished between laws and customs – leges et consuetudines. At that time it was a generally established rule that laws were as a rule issued only when it was necessary to change or replace certain customs or usages so that they would meet new needs. Customs and usages that suited the magnates and that were in use naturally did not need to be fixed separately in statutory form. Since the record was made only 16 years after the rise of Great Moravia, it may be assumed that the customs and usages mentioned go back to still earlier times.
The imperfect picture of law and of procedure in the secular courts – the so-called
placita secularia

– in Great Moravia can at least in part be filled out from fragmentary data in the chronicles, chiefly those of East Frankish provenance, and further by comparison with certain institutions of the oldest Czech, Slavic in general and Hungarian legal monuments. Among the Hungarian legal monuments there is, for example, the so-called
Regestum Varadiense
, which was in fact a record of the ordeals that had been carried out. The very designation of the court tribunal concerned –
iudicium ad praudam

/pravdam/ – testifies that it arose in the period before the Kingdom of Hungary came into being. Its direct relationship to Great Moravia, or rather to the Nitra region, is given by the fact that the limits of this tribunal’s jurisdiction reached as far as the border zone that separated it from the Nitra region. This is finally also suggested by the statutes of the Hungarian king Coloman, which permitted these „iudicia“ to be held only in episcopal seats, the exception being precisely Nitra and Bratislava, for the reason that as a seat of judgement they already had a great tradition. It is very probable that some of the old Slavic terms and provisions of the so-called Statutes of Duke Conrad Otto /Statuta ducis Ottonis/, issued probably at the end of the 12th century, also have a certain connection with Great Moravian law. They have survived, however, in three later redactions, namely for the appanage of Znojmo /1222/, of Brno /1229/ and of Břeclav /1123/, that is, precisely for the former central areas of the Great Moravian state. These are, for example, the old legal terms: nárok /nárok/, which is also given in Methodius’s translation of the nomocanon, further zok /sok/, druho /druh/, zuod /svod/, powod /pôvod/, zlubni zud /sľubný súd/, Wiboy /výboj/, hirdozt /hrdosť/, wrez /vrez/, pohonce /póhončie/, nestoite /nestojte/, kiy /kyj/. But they are also regulations on the ordeals /iudicium ferri; compare also Cosmas’s chronicle, iudicium aguae/. The role of the vetula /the old woman/ in these ordeals probably also has very old roots, as do the provisions on witnesses /"sub testimonio ... probos viros“, which have much in common with the relevant provisions of the Zakon sudnyj ljudem and with the so-called Methodian homily /from the Glagolita Clozianus collection/. From the sphere of state administration the suppani are recalled /župans, who are likewise named in the Zakon sudnyj ljudem/. Among the Czech legal monuments the so-called Book of Rožmberk should also be further examined from this aspect.

children.text: Frankish sources likewise testify that in Great Moravia the means of proof used were „
ordeals of God“ /ordeals
/ or
the oath

, which, however, also served to secure an obligation, besides the giving of the hand or, as the case might be, the handing over of hostages. A very frequently used institution was asylum. Banishment was also used as a punishment. The execution of the sentence was ensured by the organs of public power, bailiffs and mercenaries, and by the appropriate equipment: dungeons, prisons, iron fetters, stocks and so on.

In the border areas the Frankish comites sought to gain influence over Moravian justice. In general it may be assumed that the influence of Frankish law was comparatively great, even if it was not welcome. Byzantine influence was, however, also significant /the reception of Byzantine law/. According to the convincing linguistic evidence of J. Vašica, the so-called Zakon sudnyj ljudem /the oldest known Slavic legal monument/ must be regarded as a work created for Great Moravia at the request of Rastislav and his magnates, or rather his župans, by Constantine together with Methodius, roughly in the second half of the 9th century /after the arrival of their mission in Moravia in 863/.
Zakon sudnyj ljudem

was drawn up by its authors on Byzantine models, chiefly on the so-called Ecloga, though with certain marked changes and additions of a Western Roman, or rather Slavic, character. In its 33 articles the Zakon sudnyj ljudem contains above all provisions of criminal law: offences against the faith, against morality and offences against property – theft and arson – and further the right of asylum, provisions on the division of war booty and on witnesses. From private law these are above all the provisions on family law /monogamous marriage and its impediments, separation, etc./, further commodatum /similar to the relevant articles of the laws of King Ladislaus in Hungary/ and compensation for damage, and finally also the provisions on the ransoming of prisoners of war.

The deviations of the ZSL text from the Byzantine Ecloga mentioned above are highlighted in the so-called Anonymous – also Methodian – homily /from the Glagolita Clozianus collection/, which is a kind of exhortation to the princes acting as judges to observe the provisions of the ZSL. These were above all the following changes, brought about mainly by the reception of the provisions of Western Roman canon law: the active participation of witnesses in the proceedings, the replacement of the cruel corporal punishments of the Ecloga by ecclesiastical fasts, and the prohibition of pagan oaths and usages. In addition, this homily emphasised certain further provisions and regulations of the ZSL that were significant from the point of view of the Church, such as: impartiality in the courts, the prohibition of marriage between persons spiritually related, the principle of monogamous marriage and its indissolubility, and above all the supremacy of the so-called „divine“, ecclesiastical laws over secular laws.

The comparatively incomplete systematics and likewise the very content of this law, which regulated or altered above all such legal relations as were of eminent interest to the Church, testify that the Zakon sudnyj ljudem was probably used in Great Moravia only as a supplementary and
auxiliary norm of an already existing body of law of their own and of the legal order in general, the basis of which was customary law

. The Zakon sudnyj ljudem testifies not only to the existence but also to the viability of a legal system of their own. This Slavic–Moravian law not only did not succumb as a whole to the reception of the advanced Byzantine law, but on the contrary creatively transformed some of its provisions in accordance with its own institutions and with overall social relations in general.

Important monuments of canon law have also survived from this period. Besides the already mentioned so-called Anonymous, or rather Methodian, homily, it was above all Methodius’s translation of the so-called
Nomocanon

. The model for this translation was for Methodius a Byzantine collection of canon law whose author was the Constantinopolitan patriarch John Scholasticus, namely the so-called Synagoge in 50 titles, which was recognised not only by the Eastern Roman but also by the Western Roman Church, and was therefore suitable for Great Moravia as well. Even so, Methodius shortened his nomocanon by 142 canons; the Synagoge had 377 of them. The translation of the nomocanon contains the following terms, which are perhaps of Moravian origin: „istina“ /in the sense of a stolen thing/ – this term also occurs in the Czech Book of Rožmberk – further „rok“ /also given by the Chronicle of Dalimil/, „nárok“ /also given by the Book of Rožmberk and the Statutes of Duke Conrad Otto/, „obrok“, „uvarovati“ /a child/ and so on. From the sphere of state organisation these are the terms „snem“ /also in the Lives of Constantine and Methodius/, „oblasť“ and „predel“ /compare medza, meza/.
Another important collection of canon law, this time of an expressly Western Roman character, is the so-called
Collectio canonum

/also the „Expanded Hadriana“/, which Methodius received from the Pope on one of his journeys to Rome in order to strengthen his archiepiscopal, metropolitan authority over the bishops subordinate to him, his suffragans. The Collectio canonum is significant also because it contains the oldest known Slavic glosses, the so-called Emmeram glosses /the canon glossed is 35.34./, „De primatu episcoporum“. Ecclesiastical canon law, and even the precepts of the Bible, generally had a great influence on secular law and especially on procedure.
Zakon sudnyj ljudem (Great Moravia, 9th century)

blocks.text:
1. Before any law code, mention must be made of God’s truth. Therefore Saint Constantine in the first law wrote and spoke thus: Every village in which pagan sacrifices or oaths are performed shall be handed over to the temple of God together with all the property that belongs to the lords in that village. Those who perform the sacrifices and the oaths shall be sold together with all their property, and the proceeds obtained shall be given to the poor.
2. In every dispute, suit and accusation it must be observed that the prince and the judge do not accept an accusation without hearing many witnesses. It must be said to the parties, to the plaintiffs and to the accusers: If you cannot prove it with the help of witnesses, as the law of God also commands, expect to receive the same punishment as you have pronounced against the other. So commands the law of God, and whoever does not keep it, let him be accursed.
3. On booty. He who has set out against the enemy into battle shall guard himself against all evil words and deeds. He shall keep God in mind, pray, and wage the battle with prudence. For help from God is received by those who have prudent hearts. For victory does not rest in an exceeding multitude of strength, because strength is from God. If God grants victory, let the prince take the sixth part, and let all the people divide the remainder in equal shares, whether they be great or small. For the princely share and the increase of the pay of their men shall suffice for the župans. If there be found among them any, whether elders or common soldiers, who through courage and valour perform heroic deeds, let the prince or the voivode who is present add to them from the princely share, as is fitting, in order to distinguish them. The same sum as is received by those who took part in the battle shall also be received by those who remained in the camp. For thus spoke, wrote and ordained the prophet David.
4. He who has a wife of his own and sins with a female slave: if this offence is proved, it is necessary that the prince of that land sell her into another land, and the sum obtained for her is to be divided among the poor. Likewise the fornicator shall, according to the law of God, be placed by the prince at the disposal of the priests for a seven-year penance: for two years let him stand before the temple of God during the mass; for two further years let him enter the temple for the reading of the gospel and spend the rest of the mass outside, listening to the mass; and for another two years he may remain until the Creed. In the last, seventh year let him stand in the temple, but let him not receive communion. When the seven years have passed, in the eighth year let him receive communion at last. (Those condemned) are obliged to eat nothing but bread and water for seven years.
5. He who sins with another man’s female slave shall pay 30 gold pieces to the slave’s master, and shall himself undergo a seven-year penance, as we have already said, so that he be not fined. If he is poor, let him pay the slave’s master according to the (size of) his property, and let him himself undergo the fast mentioned.
6. He who commits fornication with a nun shall, according to secular law, have his nose cut off; according to ecclesiastical law, however, let a fifteen-year penance be imposed on him.
7. He who takes as his wife the mother of his godchild: according to secular law the noses of both of them are cut off and they are separated. According to ecclesiastical law let them be separated and let them undergo a penance of 15 years. The order of the fast is as follows: for five years to stand outside (before the temple) weeping and to listen to the mass; then for four years they may be in the temple until the holy gospel, and for three years until the Creed, and for a further three years until the end of the mass, on bread and water. And so, when they have completed the term of the fast, in the sixteenth year let them receive communion. Let the same punishment befall him who marries his goddaughter or sins with a married woman.
7a. On witnesses. In the case of all these (offenders) the prince and the judge shall, in every dispute, conduct the investigation with all care and patience and shall not condemn without witnesses. Witnesses must be sought who are truthful, God-fearing, respected, and such as have no hatred nor malice, nor anger, nor dispute, nor accusation against him about whom they testify, but only the fear of God and of his justice. Let the number of witnesses be eleven or even more than this number. In a small dispute from seven to three, but not fewer than this number. The judge, however, has the power to accept a pledge from the man against whom they testify, and to impose an oath upon the witnesses, or also a fine, or the same punishment, if it should at any time appear that they have lied. In no dispute shall those be accepted as witnesses who have at any time been convicted of lying or of transgressing the law of God, or who lead a depraved life, or who are excluded from the oath as incapable.
8. When someone has seduced a maiden without the consent of her parents and they learn of it afterwards: if he wishes to take her and her parents also wish it, let the wedding be held. If, however, one of them refuses, and he is a (man) respected for his wealth, let him give the girl a litra of gold for the dishonour, that is, 72 gold solidi. If he is poorer, let him give half his property. If, however, he is without means, let the judge have him flogged and expelled from his district. He is also obliged to undergo a penance for seven years, as we have written.
9. He who has raped a maiden in a deserted place, where there was no one who could help her, shall be fined, and his property shall be given to the girl.
10. He who has seduced an adolescent girl before she has completed her thirteenth year shall be fined (by the loss) of all his property, and the proceeds from it shall be given to the girl. According to ecclesiastical law, he and the man who has done violence to a girl betrothed to a man are all subject to a seven-year penance, as we have already mentioned above in the case of a married woman.
12. Those guilty of incest, who have contracted marriage with blood (relatives), shall be separated.
13. He who has two wives shall drive out the one he took later, together with her children. Then let him be flogged and let him do penance for seven years.
14. He who sets fire to another man’s wood or fells trees in it shall pay twofold compensation.
15. He who out of enmity or for the sake of plundering property sets fire to dwelling houses shall be burned, if it is in a town. If it is in a village or on a homestead, let him be executed by the sword. But according to ecclesiastical law he is handed over for a penance of 12 years, for he is an enemy. If someone wishes to burn stubble or brushwood on his own land and kindles a fire, and it leaps across and sets alight another man’s field or another man’s vineyard, the whole matter must be judged and investigated. If it came about in such a way that he kindled the fire out of ignorance or thoughtlessness, let him compensate the injured party. If he were to kindle a fire on a windy day, or did not take the necessary precautions, saying: the fire will not spread, or out of idleness, or because he cannot, and the fire causes damage, let him pay and let him be flogged. If, however, he observed all precautions and a storm suddenly came, and the fire therefore spread widely, let him not be condemned. If someone’s house catches fire from lightning and either his own dwelling burns down, or the fire spreads and the houses of his neighbours burn down as well, then, because this fire arose unexpectedly, he is not to be tried.
16. Let no one lead out of the temple by force him who has taken refuge in it. He who flees here shall acquaint the priest with his affair and with the guilt he has committed. Let the priest receive him as a fugitive, so that his crime may be investigated and examined according to the law. If anyone, whoever he may be, attempts to lead out of the temple by force the man who has taken refuge here, let him receive 140 strokes of the rod. Then let the crime of him who has taken refuge here be duly examined.
17. If someone has a dispute with another and does not report it to the vladykas and pursues the dispute to his own harm, wishing to press his purpose either by might or by violence: if he does so, then even if he is in the right, let him lose his case and let him return it. If he were to take something belonging to another, let the vladyka of that region beat him with the rod, because he does not submit to authority and makes himself his own avenger. And if he acts in this way, let him return what he has taken.
18. If parents and children contradict one another, let them not be believed. And neither in a master’s favour nor against him shall a slave or a freedman appear as a witness.
19. If someone buys a prisoner of war from foreign soldiers and takes him into his house, then, if the prisoner has with him the sum for which he was bought, let him give it for himself and he may depart freely.
20. Witnesses by hearsay shall not testify, and shall not say: We have heard from someone that this man is a debtor, or testify about anything else from hearsay. Nor shall they testify in the case where župans are concerned.
21. Soldiers who were taken prisoner and denied their Christian faith shall, on returning to their own country and to their civil rights, be handed over to the Church.
22. If someone borrows a horse for a journey to a certain place, or sends it, and it happens that the horse is injured or dies, the borrower must compensate the owner of the horse.
24. He who steals in war: if it is a weapon, let him be beaten. If it is a horse, let him pay a fine.
25. If a master wishes to keep such a slave as steals, let him make good the damage. If he does not wish to keep this slave any longer, let him hand him over into slavery to the man who was robbed.
26. He who drives away another man’s herd: if he has done it for the first time, let him be beaten. If he has done it a second time, let him be banished from the land. If he has done it a third time, let him be subjected to punishment, but only after he has returned everything he drove away.
27. He who strips the dead in the grave shall be punished.
28. He who breaks in to the altar by day or by night and takes something from the sacred vessels or vestments, or any other thing whatsoever, shall be punished. He who takes something from the other parts of the church shall be beaten with the rod, shorn and banished from the country as a godless man.
29. He who seizes a free man and sells him or enslaves him shall himself be enslaved, since he too has enslaved a free man; let him himself taste slavery.
30. He who entices another man’s slave to himself, hides him and does not say where he is, is obliged to return him to his master, or to give him another, or his price.
30a. The dispute of spouses. The wisdom of the Creator and Saviour, our Lord God, teaches us that married cohabitation is by God indissoluble. For he, when he created man, who did not exist, into being, did not create the woman in the same way, by taking clay from the earth, although he could have done so, but took a rib from the man and created her, so that in this way, wisely, by the joining of one flesh in two persons, he might make indissoluble marriage law. Therefore he did not separate from the man even the woman who, when through the cunning of the devil she began to taste bitterness, gave the man also to taste of it. Nor did he separate from the woman the man who together with his wife transgressed the commandment of God, but he punished them for that sin with suffering. Their marriage, however, he preserved. By this law, then – already revealed and confirmed by the gospel at the time when the Pharisees asked Christ our God whether it is permitted to put away one’s own wife for every sin, and Jesus answered: What God has joined together, let not man put asunder, save for the cause of adultery – we too are guided as true disciples of Christ our God, and we do not venture to enact anything else. Since, however, the devil sows hatred between spouses on account of accusations, or of carnal or other vices, we therefore establish by law the following among the causes for which spouses are separated: a man shall be separated from his wife for such a sin, if the wife is convicted of having plotted against his life, or also if she learned of any evil deeds of other persons directed against her husband and did not inform him of it, or if she falls into the disease of leprosy. A woman shall be separated from her husband if he plots against her, or if he knows of it from others and does not tell her, and likewise if he falls into the disease of leprosy. And also in the case where one of them falls into a grave disease before marital intercourse. All this it belongs to the prince and to the judges to investigate with witnesses, as we have written about it above, before the judgement of God, where all human vices are to be judged by the princes. And therefore we must have regard for no one, but must teach all men day after day in the law of God and hope in Christ our God that at the last judgement we shall hear the blessed voice: Come, blessed and faithful servants, I shall set you over many things, enter into the joy of the Lord your God and rejoice with the angels for ever and ever.

children.text: A comparison of selected provisions with the law in force in the Slovak Republic:

Section 127(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure: Everyone is obliged to appear upon a summons of the bodies active in criminal proceedings and of the court and to testify as a witness about what is known to him concerning the criminal offence and the offender, or concerning circumstances important for the criminal proceedings.

Section 346(1) of the Criminal Code: Whoever, as a witness in proceedings before a court or in criminal proceedings, or for the purposes of criminal proceedings abroad before a prosecutor or a police officer, or before a judge of an international body recognised by the Slovak Republic, states an untruth about a circumstance of substantial significance for the decision, or whoever conceals such a circumstance, shall be punished by imprisonment for one to five years.
Section 203 of the Criminal Code: "Whoever has sexual intercourse with a relative in the direct line or with a sibling shall be punished by imprisonment for up to two years."
Section 204 of the Criminal Code: "Whoever, during the subsistence of his marriage, contracts another marriage shall be punished by imprisonment for up to two years."
What is evidently meant here is not the seizing of the enemy’s property, but of property belonging to the soldiers of one’s own army. Today this is in practice theft.
Section 212(1) of the Criminal Code: "Whoever appropriates another’s property by taking possession of it and thereby causes minor damage shall be punished by imprisonment for up to two years"

Section 365(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure: "Whoever destroys, damages or desecrates a grave, an urn with human remains, a monument or a gravestone, or destroys or damages the equipment of a burial ground or of another place of final rest, or whoever commits other gross indecency or disorderly conduct at a burial ground or at another place of final rest, shall be punished by imprisonment for up to two years. But at the same time it is also a classic theft"
(Family law, the dissolution of marriage, relations between spouses – the Family Act)
